"Javits Frimpong’s mother deserves to say goodbye to her son in person. I just got off the phone with President Trump, and he has agreed to grant her visa immediately."

articles.title: Deal worth £12bn to build windfarms off Norfolk coast
articles.summary: Prime Minister Andy Burnham says the investment is "a vote of confidence for building in Britain".
articles.body:
A £12bn deal to construct wind farms has been described by Prime Minister Andy Burnham as "a vote of confidence for building in Britain".

Energy company RWE and investment firm KKR have announced the funding, which will deliver the Vanguard West and Vanguard East offshore wind farms off the Norfolk coast.

The wind farms are expected to be fully commissioned in 2030, with offshore construction scheduled to begin in early 2027.

"It is great news for billpayers because every turbine we put up is power under British control, not at the mercy of events on the other side of the world," added Burnham, as he prepared to head to the Cop31 climate summit.

"With coastal communities from Scotland to East Anglia powering Britain's future, the places that host this energy benefit from the jobs and opportunities that it brings," he added.

The financing includes £1bn from the state-owned National Wealth Fund, which Burnham said was "working alongside private capital to build homegrown energy and bring a return for the taxpayer".

Burnham will join other world leaders at the United Nations' Cop31 summit in Antalya, Turkey, where he will deliver a speech on Thursday.

German firm RWE said the Vanguard projects, located between 50 and 80 km (31 to 49 miles) off the coast, represented one of the UK's largest offshore wind developments, generating around 2.8 gigawatts, enough to supply three million homes.

It bought the sites, and a third offshore site - Norfolk Boreas - in 2023, when work on that development had been paused by its then owner, Vattenfall.

The government said the investment would support more than 2,400 jobs in the construction and operation phases.

Preparatory work was already well advanced, including onshore cable installation activities and construction of the substations, RWE added.

RWE chief executive Markus Krebber said: "Together with KKR, we are delivering two of the UK's largest offshore wind projects, strengthening domestic electricity generation and making an important contribution to the country's long-term energy security."

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said: "As the world gathers at Cop31, Britain is leading from the front as a renewable energy powerhouse, turning the fight against climate change into a brighter future for British companies, industrial communities, and future generations."

articles.title: Texas Roadhouse goes beyond steak with new menu addition that has some fans questioning the move
articles.summary: Chicken Alfredo Pasta is being added to over 600 Texas Roadhouse locations as the chain is testing energizer drinks and mocktails across all three of its brands.
articles.body: Texas Roadhouse is expanding its Chicken Alfredo Pasta rollout and testing new nonalcoholic drinks across its three restaurant brands, according to a report. The steakhouse chain added Chicken Alfredo Pasta to more than 600 locations in recent months and plans to bring it to the roughly 100 remaining locations by spring 2027, executives said during the company's third-quarter earnings call, Nation's Restaurant News reported. Operators had asked for a new menu item, and early tests of the pasta proved popular with customers and staff, CEO Jerry Morgan said. MAN SAYS TEXAS ROADHOUSE SERVED HIM $20 STEAK INSTEAD OF PRICIER FILET MULTIPLE TIMES "It's a great choice for somebody who wants something a little bit different," Michael Bailen, vice president of investor relations for Texas Roadhouse, said. Individual locations shared news of the penne pasta dish online, describing it as "creamy, cheesy and seriously delicious." Some fans praised the dish, with one woman on Facebook saying it was "so good" and that she hoped it would remain on the menu permanently. MEAT EXPERT SHARES THE MISTAKE MOST AMERICANS MAKE WHEN COOKING STEAK Others, however, wondered what a pasta dish was doing on a steakhouse menu. "Who goes to a steakhouse and orders chicken Alfredo?" one Reddit user said in a thread dedicated to Texas Roadhouse. Bailen said the dish is "probably not going to be one of our top 10 mix entrée items that we offer, but it rounds out the menu." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Texas Roadhouse is also seeing continued demand for mocktails and dirty sodas, according to the report. The company is now testing "energizer" drinks at all three of its brands: Texas Roadhouse, Bubba's 33 and Jaggers. The menu moves come as the company works to maintain momentum after sales growth slowed late in the third quarter, according to Nation's Restaurant News. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Executives attributed part of the slowdown to a viral social media hoax that falsely accused Texas Roadhouse and Logan's Roadhouse employees of planning to tamper with Black customers' food. The company investigated and concluded the claims were false. Sales and traffic improved each week in October and continued to strengthen in early November, executives said. Texas Roadhouse expects to open approximately 35 company-owned restaurants across its three brands in 2026, with another 35 planned for 2027. articles.title: F1 champion Lewis Hamilton calls on Israel to open Gaza’s Rafah border
articles.summary: Hamilton visited the Egypt-Gaza border as conditions worsened for Palestinians in Gaza after heavy rains.
articles.body:
Seven-time Formula One champion Lewis Hamilton has called on Israel to reopen the Rafah crossing to allow humanitarian supplies into Gaza from Egypt, amid worsening conditions after heavy rains and flooded makeshift camps.

The remarks came on Wednesday, a day after the British F1 driver visited Egypt’s northern city of el-Arish, which borders Gaza, touring a storage facility where the Egyptian Red Crescent had prepared boxes of aid to be sent to Palestinians in the besieged enclave.

In a post on social media, Hamilton said, “People in Gaza and Palestine are in such urgent need that they could hardly need this aid more than they do right now.”

“That’s why we really need to put pressure on Israel and work together to make sure this aid reaches them,” he said.

Hamilton said there were warehouses storing essential supplies in several locations, but the supplies were not reaching Palestinians who need them because of the border closure.

A post on Hamilton’s Instagram page showed him meeting some of the volunteers and workers for the Egyptian Red Crescent, as well as stationary trucks loaded with food waiting to cross the border.

“The past three years of Israel’s genocide in Gaza is appalling. It’s an injustice for people to being denied their freedom, their safety and their dignity. No human being should be treated as though their life matters less,” Hamilton said.

Meanwhile, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu rejected accusations that Israel has been delaying the entry of winter supplies into the Gaza Strip.

More than 150,000 tents bought by humanitarian partners and member states are waiting outside the Gaza Strip for Israeli permission to enter, the United Nations said on Wednesday.

UN humanitarian chief Tom Fletcher said on Wednesday that waiting for a new Israeli government to form is “not an acceptable excuse” for delays in getting essential winter supplies into Gaza.

articles.title: Foreign spy ‘honeytraps’ targeting America’s tech elite spark alarm amid Nvidia CEO scandal
articles.summary: Jensen Huang's relationship with alleged Chinese intelligence asset Alice Huang raises urgent questions about honeytrap espionage targeting Silicon Valley.
articles.body: American tech executives are facing escalated and systematic campaigns by foreign intelligence services using a variety of spy tactics to get the upper hand, including "honeytraps," to infiltrate U.S. expert controls, supply chains and other intelligence, experts say. The warning comes amid reports revealing NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang's extramarital relationship with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom U.S. intelligence identified as a Chinese intelligence asset operating under corporate cover. Foreign espionage operations targeting high-profile tech figures are not isolated incidents but reflect an ongoing, long-term threat designed to exploit business environments, former National Security Agency analyst and corporate cybersecurity expert Ira Winkler told Fox News Digital. articles.title: Pope Leo returns to a national celebration in his second homeland of Peru
articles.summary: LIMA, Peru — Pope Leo XIV arrived in his second homeland of Peru on Wednesday, returning to the place that he credits with teaching him how to be a pastor and where a nationwide party awaits to welcome their beloved “Padre Robert” home.
articles.body: LIMA, Peru — Pope Leo XIV arrived in his second homeland of Peru on Wednesday, returning to the place that he credits with teaching him how to be a pastor and where a nationwide party awaits to welcome their beloved “Padre Robert” home. The visit to Peru marks the final leg of Leo’s three-nation South America tour and its emotional highlight, given the more than two decades that the former Robert Prevost spent in Peru as a missionary priest and later bishop. As a dual citizen of the United States and Peru, he’s the first pope from each country. Leo’s charter plane touched down at a Lima-area air base, where he was welcomed by President Keiko Fujimori. Leo seemed genuinely moved as he emerged from his Aerolineas Argentinas charter plane, smiling broadly as he greeted Fujimori and embracing two children who brought him flowers. From his open-sided popemobile, he greeted tens of thousands of spectators lining the streets for several miles and waving Peruvian and Holy See flags to welcome the pope back to the country he says taught him “what it means to be a shepherd.” Some in the roaring crowds broke the established protocol and tight security to chase behind the car that transported him to the presidential palace. “We love him so much because he’s worked here, he knows our sufferings, he knows it all,” said 85-year-old Evelina Cruz, who held a pope plush doll made by her niece. Elation over the pope’s return felt across Peru “My heart is so excited that it makes me want to cry with joy,” said Zuly Castillo, who served as Leo’s secretary when he was bishop of the northern city of Chiclayo near the Pacific Coast. Across from her office, a life-size cardboard cutout of the pope now welcomes visitors to his former residence. “Peru is the crown of the trip, the homecoming of the first Peruvian pope, no matter where he was born,” said Gustavo Morello, an associate professor of sociology at Boston College and the author of “Lived Religion in Latin America.” “This is a return to his origins without any doubt,” Morello said. In preparation for the pope’s visit, a huge 46-foot statue of the pontiff was unveiled in the port of El Callao. Baristas in Lima, the capital, were offering cappuccinos decorated with the image of the pope. With hands raised and voices lifted in song, hundreds awaited the pope’s arrival in Lima in front of the presidential palace, where a stage and giant screens had been set up amid tight security. “Long live Christ!” the crowd sang, following a Catholic choir on the stage. “It’s so beautiful and so moving,” said Anni Marino, 52, who enthusiastically joined the singing. “I hold it in my heart because he’s the representative of God.” Popemania also hit Chiclayo. Leo is painted in colorful murals, emblazoned on T-shirts, baseball hats, and even bobblehead dolls and ice creams. Leo will celebrate Mass in all his old stomping grounds including at the nearby sanctuary of St. Turibius of Mogrovejo in Zaña, a city that is a hub of Afro-Peruvian culture, and where the pope often visited to pray to the saint of his devotion. Since Leo knows his adopted country so well, his speeches will be closely watched, especially one he’ll deliver from the square in front of Lima’s cathedral “on the challenges and hopes for the future of the Peruvian people.” Peru hit by poverty and political instability Peru, a nation of 34 million people, is overwhelmed by challenges, among them the looming arrival of nature’s chaotic climatic agent of El Niño, violent crime and income inequality. In 2025, 25.7% of the Peruvian population was living in monetary poverty. “A small elite has GDP levels comparable to some U.S. states,” Morello said, adding that while the macroeconomy “is doing well, most Peruvians live in structural poverty and economic insecurity.” “This could help build stability in the political system. Without any doubt, Peru is better now than 30 years ago, when Shining Path was still a threat,” he said about the rebel movement that terrorized Peru in the 1980s and 1990s when Leo was a young Augustinian missionary. “His return, now as pope, inspires great hope among a large segment of Peruvian society that still perceives and feels the abandonment of the state,” said Rolando Pérez, a professor at the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru. “Deeply etched in the public consciousness is the image of a shepherd who stood by the people, helping to bring into the public agenda their demands and their cry for justice,” he said. Honoring Indigenous in the Amazon and threats of flooding The pope will honor Peru’s Indigenous peoples by traveling to Pucallpa, in Peru’s Amazon, to celebrate Mass. Illegal gold mining and the cultivation of coca leaves, the raw material used to produce cocaine, are affecting Peru’s Indigenous peoples. “The Amazon is a place where critical issues affecting development -- such as the environmental crisis, the exclusion of Indigenous peoples, various forms of violence, and extreme poverty-- all intersect,” said Pérez. Leo will also meet with popular groups of faithful and representatives of local traditions in Cusco — the capital of the Inca empire, an important city of Spanish colonial rule and an important cultural destination, including the nearby ruins at Machu Picchu. The pope will celebrate Mass in Cusco’s main square, where in 1781 the Indigenous hero Túpac Amaru II was killed following the most significant rebellion against the Spanish during the colonial era. Political instability and calls for answers The conservative Fujimori came to power in July on promises of restoring order to a nation plagued by extortion and homicide, which have nearly doubled, reaching 10.7 per 100,000 inhabitants -- up from 5.8 five years ago. Cárdenas said Peruvians will welcome the pope at a time when many feel disappointed with authorities following a decade of political instability that has seen a revolving door of nine presidents since July 2016. Many Peruvians are also battered by rising insecurity and the increasing cost of food. “There’s no sign of a reaction, no strategy,” from Fujimori’s government, he said. As a result, many hope for a message from Leo that will prompt a response from those in power. “There’s a profound sense of weariness regarding politics and corruption,” said Véronique Lecaros, head of the department of theology at the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru. In contrast, she said the Catholic church enjoys a level of credibility that surpasses any other Peruvian institution. Huge crowds are expected to turn out to welcome Leo home, even though Peru has seen Catholicism fall in recent years. According to the Pew Research Center, the Catholic population was at 76% in 2013-2014, but now stands at around 67%. That stands in line with trends around the world where many continue to join the growing ranks of the religiously unaffiliated. Known as the “nones,” they identify as atheists, agnostics, spiritual but not religious, or simply, nothing in particular. But Lecaros says this doesn’t mean Peruvians have lost their faith, and most still consider themselves to be religious. “They’ll listen to the pope, and some inspired by his example, will renew their interest in the church,” she said. “In the end though, it will depend on how Catholic lay and clerical leaders choose to behave.”

articles.title: Millions of Spaniards stage first general strike in 14 years as anger rages over housing
articles.summary: Four million Spanish workers took part in a general strike on Wednesday, unions said, enduring stormy weather to set up picket lines in a protest against the country’s housing affordability crisis less than three weeks before a snap general election.
articles.body: Four million Spanish workers took part in a general strike on Wednesday, unions said, enduring stormy weather to set up picket lines in a protest against the country’s housing affordability crisis less than three weeks before a snap general election. It is the first general strike since workers downed tools in 2012 against austerity measures during the euro zone debt crisis. The walkout is backed by Spain’s two largest unions, UGT and CCOO, representing more than a million workers, as well as tenants’ associations angry about rising rents and evictions. Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez hopes to harness voter resentment over housing in the November 29 election to shift the political narrative away from corruption cases involving his inner circle and a deadly train crash last month. So far, his Socialist Party still trails in opinion polls. Unions described the strike as a success even though participation was uneven across Spain, with the strongest support in coastal regions where housing pressures have been particularly acute. Shops shuttered On Madrid’s Gran Via, one of the capital’s main shopping streets, protesters cheered as stores including Primark, H&M and Pull & Bear drew their shutters amid a heavy riot police presence. “We’re going to close the Mango store,” the protesters chanted as they jangled sets of house keys above their heads. Many shops in Barcelona were also closed and boarded up in anticipation of unrest. Spain has a deficit of about 750,000 homes, which is set to grow to more than a million by 2028, according to the central bank. With fewer people able to afford a home, renting has increased sharply, putting pressure on that market. The average rental price of €1,176 ($1,315) is equivalent to about 98.7% of a young person’s average monthly salary in Spain, according to the Youth Council of Spain. “I’m 36 years old and I still can’t move out on my own,” said Madrid resident Jesus Gonzalez, who works in a hospital IT department and supports the strike. “Rents just keep going up, house prices just keep going up, and it’s simply impossible.” Turnout strongest at ports, auto plants Angela de Miguel, vice president of Spain’s main business lobby CEOE, said the strike was counterproductive because small businesses were also affected by the housing crisis, since shortages of homes made recruitment more challenging. Speaking on state broadcaster TVE, she said the solution was to build more homes and to lower taxes in construction and the home-buying process. Plans for massive protest marches in the afternoon were threatened by two heavy storms, dubbed Charles and Bruna, with unions suspending a demonstration in the southern port city of Cadiz. The tenants’ union said it still expected participation in the strike to reach 5 million people by the end of the day. Spain has around 23 million workers, according to the national statistics institute. According to UGT and CCOO, participation in the strike reached 90% at ports and in the automotive sector, with “total stoppages” reported at factories including Volkswagen’s in Navarre and SEAT’s in Barcelona. Electricity demand dropped by as much as 15.5% between 10 a.m. and 11 a.m., according to Spain’s grid operator Red Electrica. Less impact due to remote working Barcelona’s metro said no trains would run outside peak commuting hours, while Madrid’s metro said peak-hour usage was down 42% compared to the same period last week. However, with more people able to work remotely and the increasing weight of services in Spain’s economy, the impact of the strike is likely to be less pronounced than in previous years, according to Miguel Cardoso, chief economist at BBVA Research. He estimated that the strike could shave 0.1%-0.2% off Spain’s annual gross domestic product. Spain’s fast-growing hospitality and finance industries are less unionised than the public and industrial sectors. Police had reported 40 arrests by midday from 476 incidents linked to the general strike, including blockades of offices and industrial estates and burning of rubbish containers. Unions said they would file a criminal complaint against what they described as a “disproportionate” response during a police operation involving tear gas and batons that left 20 protesters injured. The strike follows weeks of demonstrations provoked by the eviction and subsequent death of an 87-year-old woman in Madrid. Those protests, along with parliament’s rejection last month of government decrees aimed at curbing evictions and limiting rent pressures, prompted Sanchez to call the snap election.

articles.title: Fiery chaos erupts across Spain as protesters clash with police during massive nationwide strike
articles.summary: Spain's first general strike in 14 years turned violent in Barcelona as protesters set fires and launched fireworks at riot police on Paseo de Gracia.
articles.body: Unruly protesters set fires, smashed storefronts and launched fireworks at riot police across parts of Spain on Wednesday as a massive nationwide strike over soaring housing costs disrupted transportation and businesses. Violent scenes unfolded in Barcelona, where some demonstrators vandalized stores along the city's popular Paseo de Gracia shopping boulevard, set small bonfires and launched fireworks at officers arriving in riot gear and armored vehicles, according to The Associated Press. The violence erupted after a largely peaceful march as Spain experienced its first general strike in 14 years, with workers demanding relief from skyrocketing rents and the rising cost of living. TRAVELERS MAY FACE MAJOR DISRUPTIONS AS STRIKES THREATEN AIRPORTS AND POPULAR ATTRACTIONS Housing activists claimed 400,000 people marched through Barcelona, while city officials estimated attendance at 55,000. Government officials reported another 120,000 demonstrators gathered in Madrid despite heavy rain, the AP reported. The nationwide walkout disrupted public transportation, forced some businesses to close and blocked major roads. Police made arrests across the country, while officers used pepper spray against demonstrators in Madrid, according to the AP. ANGRY LOCALS BLOCK FAMOUS BEACH AS MASS TOURISM PROTESTS ESCALATE AT VACATION HOT SPOT The unrest comes amid growing frustration over Spain's housing crisis, fueled in part by the eviction of an 87-year-old Madrid woman who had lived in her apartment for seven decades before reportedly facing a tripling of her rent. She died weeks later, according to the BBC. The housing crisis has become a major political flashpoint ahead of Spain's Nov. 29 parliamentary elections, with Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez reportedly encouraging workers to exercise their right to strike. SPANISH OPPOSITION LEADER CALLS PRIME MINISTER A ‘TRAITOR’ OVER CEUTA MIGRANT CRISIS But the demonstrations have also sparked a political clash, with conservative opposition leaders accusing Sánchez's government of exploiting the unrest for electoral gain, according to the BBC. articles.title: Abandoned on London's streets at 10 and raised in more than 10 foster homes, former NFL star Efe Obada launches foundation to help young people facing similar struggles
articles.summary: For Efe Obada, life after professional American football is taking a different direction.
articles.body: For Efe Obada, life after professional American football is taking a different direction. The British-Nigerian athlete spent years building a career in the National Football League (NFL), overcoming circumstances that had once left him without a stable home, access to education or a clear route into employment. Having experienced the care system himself, he is now turning his attention towards young people facing similar difficulties.Following his retirement from professional football in 2026, Obada has established a foundation dedicated to supporting care-experienced individuals aged 11 to 25. The initiative draws on his childhood experiences and aims to give young people access to opportunities that were difficult for him to find.Efe Obada launches foundation for care-experienced young peopleObada's new foundation has been established around a problem he knows from personal experience. Having spent much of his childhood moving between foster placements, he wants to create better support for young people who are navigating life without the stability and family networks that many others take for granted.The organisation plans to use sport, education and other support services to reach individuals aged between 11 and 25. Its work is intended to help young people develop confidence, access opportunities and make decisions about their futures with greater support around them.The foundation also has ambitions beyond individual programmes. Obada wants to establish a permanent community hub in south London, providing a place where young people with experience of the care system can access services and build connections.For him, the work is closely connected to the circumstances that shaped his own childhood. Speaking to BBC Sport around the announcement of his retirement and the foundation's launch, he described the barriers and isolation associated with growing up in care as experiences he understands personally.How foster care shaped Efe Obada's early years in the UKBorn in Nigeria, Obada spent part of his early childhood with his father before being taken to the Netherlands to reunite with his mother. His life changed again when he and his older sister were brought to the UK by a stranger. The pair were around 10 and 11 years old when they were left on a street in east London.Social services subsequently became involved, and the siblings entered the care system. They remained together, but their upbringing involved repeated changes of home. Obada has spoken about living in more than 10 foster placements and encountering difficult conditions in some of them.The instability affected his education and his understanding of what life beyond childhood might look like. He was interested in studying architecture at university, but his immigration status prevented him from following that route. Without the necessary documentation, he struggled to access higher education and conventional employment.Instead, he took cash-in-hand jobs and found himself surrounded by people and circumstances that offered little stability. Looking back, he has described that period as one dominated by uncertainty and the need to get through each day.American football opened an unexpected route into the NFLBefore becoming a professional athlete, Obada was working as a security guard at a warehouse. He had no established career in American football and little reason to expect that the sport would eventually take him to the highest level.Obada joined the London Warriors in 2014 and played just five games before attracting attention from the Dallas Cowboys. Coach Aden Durde helped arrange an opportunity for him, and Dallas signed him on 1 April 2015, giving him his first NFL contract.His route into the league continued through the NFL's International Player Pathway Programme. In 2017, he joined the Carolina Panthers' practice squad through the initiative. The following year, an impressive pre-season helped him secure a place on the 53-man roster, making him the first player from the programme to achieve that milestone.He became the first player from the International Player Pathway Programme to achieve that milestone.Carolina Panthers debut brought him into the spotlightObada made his NFL regular-season debut for Carolina in 2018. His first appearance attracted attention after he recorded a sack, an interception and a forced fumble in the same game. The performance helped establish him as a player capable of competing at the professional level, despite having entered the sport relatively late and followed an unconventional route to the league.His time with the Panthers also brought him back to London for a particularly meaningful occasion. In 2019, he was named honorary captain for the team's game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium. For Obada, playing in front of friends and family in the city where his American football journey had begun carried a personal significance. He had started out with an amateur team in London only a few years earlier. Now he was representing an NFL franchise in the same city.He remained with Carolina for four seasons before moving to the Buffalo Bills in April 2021 on a one-year contract. His career later took him to the Washington Commanders, where he spent the final years of his playing career. As reported by the BBC, across his NFL appearances, Obada featured in 80 games and recorded 15 quarterback sacks. He also faced several of the league's most recognisable players, including Tom Brady, Aaron Rodgers and Drew Brees.Efe Obada wants his legacy to extend beyond his decade-long NFL careerObada's final playing chapter came with Washington. After spending the 2025 season without a team, he confirmed his retirement in 2026 at the age of 34. His professional career had lasted around a decade, during which he earned more than $8 million, according to BBC Sport. The financial security and public platform that came with playing in the NFL gave him opportunities that had seemed inaccessible during his early years in Britain.He has also spoken about the personal changes that came with his sporting career. articles.title: Stephen A Smith says white players are not good enough to win NBA championships
articles.summary: Stephen A. Smith claims the Los Angeles Lakers can't win a championship because Luka Doncic, Austin Reaves, and Walker Kessler are white.
articles.body: Luka Doncic, Austin Reaves and Walker Kessler of the Los Angeles Lakers are statistically the best overall trio in the NBA this season. Yet ESPN commentator Stephen A. Smith says the trio isn't good enough to win a championship. He doesn't cite their play as the reason, but rather their skin color. "I do not think [the Lakers] are getting past the second round. I’d be shocked if they did. I am on the record being controversially because I’ve never seen an NBA team with its top players being White deliver a championship. It’s never happened. And I’m here to tell you I don’t think it’s going to happen this year. "You can bring up whoever the hell you want," Smith said. "There has never been, in my lifetime, an NBA team led with its top three players being White that delivered you a championship when an abundance of brothers [are] playing basketball. That hasn’t happened. And I’m here to tell you it ain’t gonna happen. I can’t see it coming." Oh. Smith first made this argument in July, though he presented it differently. Then, he claimed he had "never seen" a team with three White stars win a championship. He clarified that he never said it "couldn't" happen. This time, he repeatedly dismissed the possibility of a team winning a championship led by "three White dudes." BOBBY BURACK: RYAN CLARK CLAIMS ESPN INTERVIEWED SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM ABOUT TRANS ATHLETES TO IMPRESS OUTKICK Smith provides no basketball explanation for why three White players can't lead a team to a title. articles.title: Lamps given out for seasonal affective disorder (SAD) help in winter
articles.summary: Seasonal affective disorder can affect mood, energy and sleep during the winter months.
articles.body:
The clocks have gone back, it's getting darker and colder, which could mean you may find the winter months particularly hard.

Rachel Dineem-Mabe is one of more than a million people with seasonal affective disorder (SAD) in the UK, and says it "takes depression and heightens it to a whole new level".

But a new scheme allowing people to borrow SAD lamps from libraries has been launched across Wales to help combat the darker days.

SAD happens when shorter days affect your mood, energy levels and overall wellbeing.

Rachel, 38, the branch librarian at Skewen Library, said darker days make it hard to do anything.

"I struggle just getting out of bed sometimes, I just want to hibernate," she said.

"I don't want to do anything but sleep and it is a real struggle to carry on doing normal everyday things from just dressing, not necessarily because you don't want to but you physically feel unable to."

Rachel, whose library is in one of the 11 council areas taking part in the free lamps scheme, said she notices the effects from about October.

She said: "It's a shame because it's, for me, it's a lovely time of year. I love it, but it has this low mood hanging over it that just leaves it feeling a bit sad.

"I make a real effort to get out as much as I can, obviously my job is very people focused so I'm always speaking with people which is lovely because this is a lovely community.

"I'm a big reader so that helps and I have bright lights at home like twinkly lights or ambient light all year round, to just try and boost the mood."

"I've used the SAD lamps before and it feels like just a little bit of sunshine in a day where maybe you've seen nothing, it really does boost your mood."

Rachel said that getting outside is the best advice she can give to someone experiencing SAD symptoms.

She said: "I know it's hard but get outside if you can, speak to people. Like I've said, talking about mental health is such an important thing at the moment and this is part of it.

"There are so many people who have SAD and may not even know it and it's good to acknowledge it."

Lorna Beatrice Lombardini, 26, from Cardiff Bay, said it was tough being a student during the winter months.

"You're inside a lot of the time, working deadlines, exams, and then trying to still have a social life at the same time plus work," she said.

"I absolutely love the 'say yes' idea, which is even if you get invited to plans, you're thinking it's too cold, it's too dark, I want to stay inside. Just say yes.

"Even if you go and it doesn't turn out how you want it to go, you can go home and still appreciate home that little bit more but it's always the experiences that you're not expecting that turn out to be the best."

She said she already uses lamps to help her with mood, and does feel an improvement.

"I know that this is a very universal experience but whatever I can do to try and lift the mood a little bit, feel a little bit lighter, I do try and do my best," she said.

Eleven Welsh councils are taking part in the scheme, developed by researchers from the universities of Glasgow and Edinburgh with funding from the Economic and Social Research Council.

It forms part of a wider expansion across the UK, following two years of trials in Scotland.

The lamps on loan retail at £99, but there are cheaper ones on the market.

Hester Parr, from the University of Glasgow, said the boxes available to borrow have been put together based on research of those with lived experience of SAD and contain a booklet, an online course and a lamp.

"The whole intention of the box is to help people who feel low mood in winter, or feel that they have seasonal affective disorder, make some kind of positive change," she said.

"This is outside the GP system, it's free to use from your local library, so there's no stigma attached to getting this lovely resource that helps us live well in winter."

Emily Van de Venter, from Public Health Wales, said: "People that have been part of the trials have reported benefits and wanted to continue accessing the SAD lamps, evidence has been growing around the benefits that these lamps can bring."

She advised using them for about 20 minutes in the morning, and then gain as much daylight exposure during the day as possible.

The boxes are available across Cardiff, Swansea, Wrexham, Neath Port Talbot, Blaenau Gwent, Merthyr Tydfil, Powys, Conwy, Newport, Vale of Glamorgan and Caerphilly.

If you have been affected by any of the issues in this story, support is available via BBC Action Line .

articles.title: State Department official blasts 'moronic' Washington Post report on Marco Rubio's required military flights
articles.summary: The State Department called a Washington Post report on Secretary of State Marco Rubio's military aircraft use "moronic," noting he is required to fly on government planes.
articles.body: A State Department official blasted The Washington Post on Wednesday, accusing the paper of publishing a "moronic" report that criticized Secretary of State Marco Rubio for using a military aircraft when he is required to do so. The Post published the story, "Flying by pricey military jet, Rubio rarely misses a Florida football game," which noted that the Secretary of State "is required to travel by government plane" when visiting his alma mater, where his son currently plays on the team. The piece characterized Rubio’s trips as a "cost to taxpayers," and reported that his personal flights "have cost the government more than $1.2 million." RUBIO HEADS TO ROME WITH TRUMP’S IRAN CLASH LOOMING OVER POPE, MELONI TALKS "Like the defense secretary and the directors of the FBI and CIA, Rubio is barred from flying commercially for security reasons and is required, when traveling for personal reasons, to reimburse the government the equivalent of an economy-fare ticket," wrote Post reporters Noah White and Rick Maese. "Officials’ reimbursements are rarely made public, but the amounts required cover only a fraction of the true cost, occasionally leading to scrutiny and controversy for Republican and Democratic appointees alike," they added. Rubio defended the trips, telling the paper, "I have and will continue to try and make it to as many events that are important to me personally and to my family as possible." RUBIO TO VISIT ITALY, VATICAN AMID TROOP DRAWDOWN CALL, TENSION WITH TRUMP, POPE LEO: REPORTS A government ethics expert told the Post that "Rubio’s travel complies with federal rules," but "raises a question about stewardship of public money." The Post also noted that former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg faced an audit over personal travel during the Biden administration, while pointing out that the "transportation secretary is not among the Cabinet members required to travel on military aircraft." Assistant Secretary of State for Global Public Affairs Dylan Johnson criticized the report on X, saying the "Post’s own story quotes watchdogs saying this isn’t a story and there’s nothing here." Johnson noted that the Secretary of State is required to use military aircraft, Rubio is "entirely unapologetic and will continue to attend as many of his family’s events as his jobs allow," he reimburses the government for personal travel and that the Buttigieg comparison is "moronic" because the former transportation secretary's position did not require him to use military aircraft. The State Department declined further comment to Fox News Digital. The report also drew criticism on social media. "The Washington Post is trying to make a scandal out of Secretary Rubio traveling to attend his son's football games," former White House press advisor Pat Adams wrote. "They admit he's required to travel by government plane and that his trips all comply with federal rules, but they published the story anyway to suggest impropriety." "Most parents do whatever they can to see their children compete, but the Washington Post tries to paint that as bad judgment. Completely absurd article," he added. The Post's report also noted that "senior officials have long used government planes for occasional personal travel," adding that the practice became a requirement in 1993. articles.title: Powys farmer warns Wales relies too much on imported food
articles.summary: Wales needs to grow more fruit and veg or it will be at the mercy of wars and climate change, says expert.
articles.body:
Droughts and wildfires in the summer were a wake-up call and winter flooding could leave Wales' food supply vulnerable, an expert has warned.

The country currently imports the vast majority of its fruit and vegetables, with only 6% of those served in its schools grown in Wales.

It is dependent on produce from parts of the world prone to droughts and fires, according to co-founder of an organisation aiming to address this.

Duncan Fisher is behind Our Food Trust , which wants to build 100 farms, producing fruit and vegetables in Wales for local markets.

Growers at Fisher's Wern Farm, near Newtown, Powys, said this must change if the country is to survive climate change, wars and other global disruptions to the supply chain.

"We are hugely dependent and these vegetables are coming from really vulnerable parts of the world like south Europe and north Africa - the areas most prone to drought, fires, and overheating," said Fisher.

Food security has become a hot topic , with Defence Secretary Wes Streeting saying in October people should have water, tinned goods, baby food, torches and mobile phone charging packs ready in case of emergency.

Fisher referenced this appeal, adding the UK "has an incredibly centralised food system with 95% of the food we eat bought from nine supermarkets".

He said: "There's no storage, it's a just-in-time system so the food is stored in lorries moving across motorways.

"That is a security hazard because it's very vulnerable to cyber attacks.

"If the system goes wrong, there's no resilience in it. The food just runs out straight away."

Fisher and Sue Holbrook launched Our Food Trust about 10 years ago with the aim of growing more produce locally for local markets.

They found one of the main barriers was stable housing for farmers.

As Fisher explained: "If there's a high wind during the night, they need to get out there and protect things.

"If a sheep gets in, they have to get the sheep out before the entire thing is destroyed in an hour. So they have to live there."

But he said planning regulations have made it really difficult to build homes on farmland.

However, by working with Powys council and Bannau Brycheiniog National Park Authority, they have been able to build three temporary homes for farmers on 36 acres of council-owned land.

One of the growers at Wern Farm is Lydia Dibben, 28, and she agreed access to land is one of the biggest barriers to new farmers.

She said if her home was not provided she would have to get another job to be able to afford rent, and then would end up without enough time to farm.

"I'm only growing on about just over an acre this year, and we're now doing 50 veg boxes a week," she said.

"We've been doing four farmers' markets a month up until the beginning of October. We're also supplying into regional and national wholesale as well.

"I don't know how many people we're feeding, but it's got to be hundreds of people on just a couple of acres."

She believes there are lots of people who want to do similar work, and they should be given access to land and affordable housing to do so.

Dibben said she believed people in the UK thought it would be able to "avoid many of the real challenges of climate breakdown" and "just be able to grow grapes and peaches" but the reality is very different.

"We're going to have to really think a lot harder about how we're producing food, even in this country," she said.

This includes looking at which vegetables work best in hotter climates.

Dibben described the past summer as the hardest she had experienced in five years of growing.

"The hours I was keeping were just insane," she said.

"I was getting out to the field at 05:00, and then working until it got just too hot to be outside, which was like 11:00 some days, maybe even earlier."

She said working in polytunnels was impossible by 09:00 due to the heat.

When it became too hot to work, she had to go indoors and "just survive until it was cool enough to go back outside at probably 17:00".

She then worked until midnight to try and get everything watered.

Dibben said she did not usually have to worry too much about not having enough water, but this year was completely different.

"Even the things that you felt like you were giving as much water as you could were still not growing as much as they should be," she added.

"We've not had the water bill yet for this summer, but I dread to think.

"We've just not had the crops to make it worth it."

She does not believe it will necessarily be as bad every year, but Dibben accepts there will be more hot summers and unpredictable weather such as flooding.

Dibben thinks there will always be a need for bigger scale farms producing wheat, barley, beef or sheep.

"But I think if there was a farm like ours every 10 miles throughout Wales, that would be a pretty great future in my eyes," she added.

The Welsh government said "significant progress" had been made on its plans to create a national food strategy to "target a more resilient, integrated and sustainable food system".

"There will also be a focus on how to grow more fruit and vegetables in Wales, and we have already begun mapping the current position of the sector with key stakeholders," said a spokesperson.

The UK government's Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs said: "We recognise the hurdles that our vital fruit and vegetable growers face, which is why we are slashing planning red tape and investing £200m to help farmers trial crop boosting technology.

"The prime minister has made clear that food security is national security, and we're working across the farming sector to make supply chains more resilient."

articles.title: Israeli strikes hit medical complex as nine killed across Gaza
articles.summary: Nasser Medical Complex in Khan Younis attacked as UN appeals for urgent aid to deal with heavy rains in the enclave.
articles.body:
Israeli attacks have killed at least nine Palestinians across Gaza, as the United Nations made an emergency appeal for waterproof tents to shelter hundreds of thousands exposed to flooding due to heavy rains.

At least four Palestinians were killed in an Israeli air strike on the Nasser Medical Complex in western Khan Younis, southern Gaza in the early hours of Thursday, according to Gaza’s Civil Defence spokesperson Mahmoud Basal.

An Israeli air attack on Wednesday killed 38-year-old Mohammed Salem al-Daash in the al-Sabra neighbourhood, south of Gaza City.

Another Palestinian was shot and killed by Israeli forces east of the al-Bureij camp in central Gaza, and another was killed in an Israeli drone strike in the al-Nasr neighbourhood, northwest of Gaza City.

At least two Palestinians were killed and several others wounded in a strike targeting a tent sheltering displaced people in the Sheikh Radwan neighbourhood, north of Gaza City.

Al Jazeera’s Hind Khoudary, reporting from Gaza City, described the Israeli attacks as indiscriminate targeting of civilians, saying people who were carrying on with simple attempts to survive lost their lives, such as “a man filling up a water tank, [who] was killed in a drone strike”.

“In another attack, two brothers from the al-Absi family were killed while they were sheltering inside their tent on al-Jalaa Street,” she said, adding that nowhere in Gaza was safe.

The Israeli attacks came as the UN appealed for more tents to be sent to the enclave because at least 70,000 tents were flooded in weekend rains, according to Gaza’s Government Media Office.

Heavy rain has directly affected at least 106,000 people in Gaza in recent days, according to UNICEF, with thousands of tents for displaced Palestinians submerged under water and latrines overflowing into camps.

NGOs and local organisations say they do not have the resources or capacity to deal with the crisis, as Israel continues to restrict the entry of essential aid.

“Ultimately, we need the Israeli authorities to cooperate with giving the permissions so that we can bring those tents in,” UN deputy spokesperson Farhan Haq told reporters at a media briefing, adding that apart from funding, Israeli permits were needed “to get this in”.

Certain countries supporting aid deliveries to Gaza say that delivering winter supplies will have to wait for the formation of an Israeli government, said Tom Fletcher, the UN under-secretary-general for humanitarian affairs.

In a statement, Fletcher said foreign ministers have assured their support, “but also repeatedly said that progress would be hard until after Israeli elections. Now we’re told to wait for the formation of a government”.

“This is not an acceptable excuse,” he added, citing international law and the consequences of delays, blockages and funding cuts.

Italy’s Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani said on Wednesday that Rome has launched a new emergency initiative worth 5 million euros ($5.5m) to provide immediate assistance to the Gaza Strip following the flooding.

The death toll from the Israeli genocidal war in Gaza has surged to 74,653 civilians killed since October 7, 2023, medical sources told the Palestinian Wafa news agency on Wednesday.

An additional 176,007 Palestinians have been injured in the past three years.

Israel has killed 1,622 Palestinians and injured 5,878 others since the Gaza “ceasefire” agreement came into effect on October 11, 2025.

articles.title: Hegseth and team reprimanded by Army guard at solemn war memorial
articles.summary: The guard told the defence secretary and his companions to maintain an atmosphere of "silence and respect" during a Veterans Day visit.
articles.body:
US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and members of his team were admonished by an Army guard at the Arlington National Cemetery after he and his entourage appeared to violate the solemn war memorial's rules for decorum.

A video of the Veterans Day observance event shows Hegseth, his wife and senior advisers laughing and talking while posing for photos in front of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier.

The Army sentinel on duty then steps towards Hegseth and his group and yells: "All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times."

Rules on etiquette at the cemetery dictate that visitors speak quietly and do not engage in disrespectful or disorderly conduct.

The tomb, which is one of the country's most sacred war memorials, marks the final resting place of an unknown soldier who was killed in World War I.

A service member from the 3rd Infantry Regiment stands watch over the Tomb 24 hours a day and has done so since 1948.

"While commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum," Chief Pentagon Spokesman Sean Parnell said in a statement.

"The Secretary and the entire Department have always honored—and will always honor—the sacrifices our military men and women have made to keep America safe."

Earlier, President Donald Trump, Vice-President JD Vance and other top officials attended the annual wreath-laying ceremony at the cemetery.

During his speech at the ceremony, Trump offered his gratitude to uniformed service members who have fought for the country. He also touted what he sees as his administration's success in the Iran war.

"Under this administration, and it was about time, somebody fought back. All of us fought back," he said.

"And we won," Trump said of the Iran war. "It's just a question of when we want to end it. We want to make sure we have a total victory, not a 93% victory."

Trump also pointed out Hegseth during the ceremony, saying he's done a "fantastic job" as defence secretary.

Trump has repeatedly defended Hegseth amid Democratic lawmakers' push to impeach him. On Tuesday, an effort to impeach the defence secretary under accusations that he waged war on Iran without congressional authorisation failed on Capitol Hill .

Hegseth has called the impeachment efforts a "farce" and a "stunt".

articles.title: Democrat Scott Colom wins closely watched US Senate race in Mississippi
articles.summary: The historic victory flips an eighth US Senate seat for Democrats after last week’s pivotal midterm election.
articles.body:
Democrat Scott Colom has won Mississippi’s closely watched United States Senate race, giving his party a historic victory in a Republican stronghold that has eluded them for decades.

Colom, a prosecutor, will become the state’s first Black senator in more than 140 years. On Wednesday, he narrowly defeated incumbent Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith in one of the US midterms’ biggest upsets .

The win builds on Democrats’ success after the party delivered an electoral drubbing to the rival Republicans in the November 3 midterm elections.

The left-leaning party flipped at least eight US Senate seats that are currently held by Republicans. A US Senate race in Alaska remains undecided.

For more than a week, the Mississippi contest was too close to call as election officials worked to count more than 100,000 mail-in ballots. Thousands of other residents who could not confirm their registration at voting sites cast provisional ballots that required confirmation of their eligibility.

Colom and Hyde-Smith took markedly different approaches as remaining ballots were counted.

Hyde-Smith was not seen publicly until she returned to Washington this week for the reconvening of the Senate.

Through a statement, however, Hyde-Smith and her team had expressed confidence that she would win after “every legally cast vote is fully and accurately counted”.

Colom, by contrast, has maintained a more public profile since the November 3 midterms. After the election, Colom held a series of events where he castigated his opponent.

“Ultimately, at some point, the senator needs to speak out. Where is Cindy Hyde-Smith?” Colom told reporters on Friday in Jackson, Mississippi. “We want to hear from her. She needs to answer questions. What is her path to victory? She doesn’t have one.”

The US Senate race also was not the first time the two had crossed political paths.

Hyde-Smith, citing concerns about Colom’s position on transgender athletes, had previously blocked him from serving as a federal judge in 2023 after he was nominated by former US President Joe Biden. The position had required Senate approval.

Colom’s win upturns political expectations for Mississippi, a state that US President Donald Trump won by just over 22 points in the 2024 presidential election.

The last time a Democrat won a US Senate race in Mississippi was in 1982, when John Stennis claimed victory over Republican challenger Haley Barbour, who later became governor of the state.

Colom, who has been a proponent of raising the minimum wage, increasing protections for rural hospitals and ending the US-Israel war on Iran , will be sworn in next January.

The 120th Congress will include a record number of Black senators, with seven in total.

articles.body: A Jewish doctor has been granted an exemption from union membership and fees after he challenged a requirement to financially support a union that he said violated his religious beliefs. Dr. Jacob Agronin, a physician at Temple University Hospital in Philadelphia, secured the accommodation after America First Legal (AFL) brought the matter to the Committee of Interns and Residents (CIR), Service Employees International Union (SEIU) Local 1957, demanding that the union exempt the doctor from membership and fees. AFL cited the union's stances on Israel, including endorsing the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement and accusing the Jewish state of apartheid and genocide. CIR’s collective bargaining agreement with Temple University Hospital required employees covered by the agreement to join the union or pay agency fees, according to AFL. NATION’S LARGEST TEACHERS UNION UNDER FIRE AS CONTROVERSIAL AGENDA PUTS CENTURY-OLD FEDERAL CHARTER AT RISK "[Agronin] wasn't objecting to the union's right to political speech," Megan Redshaw, counsel for AFL, told Fox News Digital. "The union can have whatever views it wants to have. However, when the union imposes its views in the workplace and that affects the people that work at that organization, that institution, or that hospital, this becomes a Title VII issue." Redshaw said Agronin believed financially supporting the union in any capacity would violate his religious beliefs, even if payments supporting political activities were excluded. The union confirmed in an Oct. 9 letter that it had granted the accommodation and that Agronin had neither signed a membership card nor paid dues. "No fees will be taken out of his paycheck, his employer will honor that and he does not have to be a member of the union at all," Redshaw told Fox News Digital. She also explained that Agronin’s request cited "Jewish law and Jewish beliefs" to explain why supporting the union conflicted with his faith. CIR says it represents "over 40,000 resident physicians and fellows who are dedicated to improving residency training and education, advancing patient care and expanding healthcare access for our communities." Redshaw accused CIR of using members’ dues to advance political and ideological causes that "nobody knows they're signing up for when they agree to join this union," while the union promotes its ability to improve pay and working conditions. POLITICAL ACTIVISM, ANTISEMITISM ALLEGATIONS PUT PUBLIC SCHOOLS UNDER THE MICROSCOPE In May 2024, CIR adopted two resolutions regarding Israel: "Housestaff for Human Rights" and "Housestaff Against Apartheid." The union stated that the first resolution "set standards to ensure CIR will not endorse candidates who accept donations from the Israel lobby or who otherwise support genocide and apartheid" and the second resolution called for a permanent ceasefire and the end of military aid to Israel. Additionally, according to the union, the "Housestaff Against Apartheid" resolution also "uplifted" the BDS movement. On Nov. 7, 2023, one month after Hamas launched its Oct. 7 attacks on Israel, CIR released a statement saying it was "appalled and shocked by the recent violence in Israel and Palestine." The union said it mourned the lives lost in the Oct. 7 attacks and those lost in the subsequent violence. In its statement, CIR called on the Biden administration and Congress to help restore access to food, water, electricity, housing and healthcare in Gaza and ensure the release of the hostages and "Palestinians detained in Israel without due process." It also urged the administration and Congress to "call for an immediate ceasefire." In May 2026, as part of his written testimony to the House Education and Workforce Committee's Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions for a hearing titled "Bad Medicine: Politics, Unions, and Antisemitism in Health Care," Agronin referenced the November 2023 statement. Agronin acknowledged the parts of the statement that "mourned Israeli and Palestinian casualties, called for hostage release and condemned antisemitism and Islamophobia," while also objecting to other parts of the statement. The physician noted that Hamas was not named in the statement, said the "Palestinian casualty figures are uncritically cited" and called the antisemitism condemnation "subordinated." CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE The physician also objected to the statement's presentation of Israeli and Palestinian casualties "in morally equivalent terms," adding that doing so "implicitly treats the perpetrators and victims of October 7th as equivalent parties." Redshaw said physicians with similar religious objections may be able to secure full exemptions from union membership and fees. "Most people believe that in requesting religious accommodation, you're just going to get an accommodation from the fees that are taken out for these political or ideological causes, or they think that that fee that's taken out has to go to a charity, usually of CIR's choosing," she told Fox News Digital. "Which is nefarious in and of itself, because the union can just choose a charity that perpetuates its causes that it believes in and transfer your money there," Redshaw added. "But the reality of this situation is that, depending on the state that you're in, you can request a full religious accommodation. You can object to being a member of the union as a whole." The Hindu calendar ties our routines to the Moon’s mood, the Sun’s rhythm, and the subtle push and pull of nakshatra energy, so we stay connected to our cultural roots while making mindful decisions. Some days are meant for gentle progress, some for bold moves, and some for patience. Let the sky’s cues help you choose better, speak softer, and act at the right moment. The Tithi running today is Shukla Paksh 3 (Tritiya), which ends at 18:09:28, after which Shukla Paksh 4 (Chaturthi) begins. Tritiya in the bright half is like the first confident sprout after the seed has taken, not yet a full plant, but clearly alive. It supports taking initiative, restarting routines, and repairing what’s been ignored. articles.body: Nvidia's board of directors is preparing to discuss the future of Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang, with the Trump administration aware of plans to remove him from the position, a CBS News reporter said in a post on X.The reported developments follow revelations about two alleged extramarital relationships involving the 63-year-old executive, one of which involved a businesswoman suspected by US intelligence officials of having links to Chinese intelligence services.The Wall Street Journal, citing people familiar with the matter, reported that Nvidia's board was preparing to meet as early as Thursday to discuss Huang's future at the company.The New York Times separately reported that Huang had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare, who reports directly to him. Citing five people who worked at the company, the newspaper said the relationship had not been previously reported.According to the report, Huang and Powell, 48, were captured on video behaving affectionately at a hotel in San Jose, California, during an Nvidia conference in March.Powell joined Nvidia in 2008 and oversees programmes focused on applying the company's chip technology to higher education and healthcare, particularly medical imaging devices, according to Nvidia's website.The reported relationship has also raised questions about the company's workplace policies. Nvidia's code of conduct asks employees to "avoid situations where our actions create conflict", including "personal relationships". The company also states that it "promptly investigates reports of misconduct", The New York Times reported, noting that several corporations have policies restricting relationships between managers and their subordinates.The latest revelations follow scrutiny of another reported relationship involving Huang and Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman associated with Singapore-based data company Megaspeed, a major Nvidia customer. US intelligence officials had identified her as an alleged Chinese intelligence asset.This was the relationship Huang acknowledged in a letter to Nvidia employees on Sunday. In the letter, he admitted being unfaithful to his wife and apologised for violating their trust.Following the acknowledgement, Nvidia's board reportedly launched an investigation into the matter, led by law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, according to The New York Times.The board was also considering Huang's position in light of the revelations involving both relationships, including the allegations concerning a possible connection to Chinese intelligence.Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and has transformed the company into a leading supplier of artificial intelligence chips, becoming one of the most prominent figures in the global AI industry.You use AI every day. articles.title: 1 dead, 12 hurt in New York City building collapse, authorities say
articles.summary: The collapse occurred around 4 p.m. in the Flatbush neighborhood. Rescuers were trying to reach people trapped in the rubble.
articles.body: One person died and 12 other people were hurt — six critically — when a building collapsed Wednesday at the edge of a construction site in New York City, a senior official said, sparking a frantic search by firefighters combing through large piles of rubble. The collapse occurred around 4 p.m. near the intersection of Bedford and Flatbush avenues in the Flatbush neighborhood of Brooklyn, the Fire Department of New York said. It was not known what caused or led up to it. The FDNY said two people were removed from the rubble soon after the collapse. Arial video showed dozens of firefighters scouring for others, with at least two who were trapped in the wreckage. A senior city official later said those two were in the process of being freed just before 5 p.m. One person died and six people were in critical condition as a result of the collapse, according to FDNY officials. Six others suffered less serious injuries, the FDNY said. Video from NBC New York’s Chopper 4 showed firefighters pulling an injured person from the rubble around 4:45 p.m. He was taken away on a stretcher. Another person was seen being taken away on a stretcher just after 6:30 p.m. The building that collapsed appeared to have been three stories tall, with a business on the ground floor. It was next to an excavation site after a one-story building that had previously been there was fully demolished. The collapsed building filled the construction pit with bricks and wood. Another building that shared a wall with the collapsed structure remained standing, but its wall was shorn off, exposing the rooms inside, including a bedroom and closets filled with clothing. The city’s Office of Emergency Management advised people to avoid the area, as traffic delays and road closures were expected. A drone hovered over the site as firefighters dug by hand, tossing chunks of rubble aside. Rescuers also used dogs to sniff for survivors. As darkness fell, firefighters used flashlights to illuminate the area where they worked. The senior city official said rescue operations were ongoing, with searches still being conducted. Phone and email messages seeking comment were left with the architect, the property owner and the general contractor listed in city records as being associated with the construction project. Multiple teams responded to the scene. An investigation continues. The Department of Buildings said inspectors were at the scene to assist with recovery operations and to conduct structural stability inspections of surrounding buildings.

articles.title: Max strength cold and flu pills – are they worth the money?
articles.summary: Some cold and flu remedies cost 20 times as much as a basic pack of paracetamol or ibuprofen.
articles.body:
But is that pricey max strength flu remedy really any better than a basic box of painkillers?

"The big brands have been around for a while, they've been tested, and there are adverts on the TV saying they're really good," says Prof Jayne Lawrence, head of the pharmacy division at the University of Manchester.

"But in reality, there's very little difference. Personally, I'd always go for the cheaper ones - and they’ve also been tested."

The trade association representing over-the-counter medicine makers says familiar brands can reassure shoppers and help them find the right product on crowded supermarket shelves.

Cold and flu drugs fall into three broad camps: household names such as Lemsip and Sudafed; supermarket own-label alternatives; and single-ingredient medicines containing paracetamol or ibuprofen.

The difference in price can be striking.

A packet of 16 Lemsip All-In-One Max Strength tablets retails at £7.30, more than 20 times the £0.35 cost of paracetamol pills in some supermarkets.

Both contain 500mg of paracetamol, which doesn't treat the underlying infection but does relieve pain and can bring down a fever.

The Lemsip version, along with many of its competitors, also contains the decongestant phenylephrine.

It's meant to constrict leaky or swollen blood vessels in the nose which can cause congestion.

But Prof Lawrence says there is little evidence it works when taken as a tablet, rather than as a nasal spray, because much of the drug is broken down before it can reach the bloodstream.

In 2024, the US drug regulator said it wanted phenylephrine removed from all cold and flu pills, saying it was simply not effective, although that proposal has yet to be finalised.

Some cold and flu remedies contain a third active ingredient - guaifenesin - which is meant to loosen mucus in the airways.

That sits in more of a grey area: some studies report improvements in chest congestion, while others find little or no benefit.

A spokeswoman for Reckitt, which owns Lemsip and Nurofen, said the ingredients in its products are approved by regulators and formulated for multiple symptoms including fever, congestion and coughs.

Many popular max strength remedies can also contain up to 65mg of caffeine per pill, about the same as a mug of instant coffee.

As well as acting as a mild stimulant, research suggests caffeine may boost the effect of paracetamol and help it work slightly sooner, although any benefit is likely to be modest.

Almost every brand can also be found as a flavoured powder to dissolve in hot water, typically costing slightly more per dose than pills or tablets.

That warm drink can be soothing and a study funded by a drug company found it may be absorbed into the bloodstream more quickly, but whether patients notice any major difference in their symptoms is much less certain.

Yet ingredients are only part of the story.

Bigger brands have more money to spend on in-store adverts and displays, according to a former manager at a large chemist chain.

Well-known names or premium own-label products are often positioned at eye level, while budget alternatives are tucked away on the bottom shelves.

"You are always going to promote the ones which are more expensive," says the former manager, who doesn't want to be named as she still works in the industry.

When it comes to medicines, some shoppers assume that paying extra means getting something more trusted or effective.

"Nine times out of ten, people would come in and ask for a certain brand," she adds.

"Even if I explained there was little difference, and I was only trying to save them money, they would still want the big name."

The PAGB, which represents the consumer healthcare sector, argues that "trusted and recognisable" brands can simplify choice and build confidence at a time when "health misinformation is widespread".

If you're suffering with cold and flu symptoms, doctors advise the following:

Rest, plenty of fluids and painkillers like paracetamol to control temperature swings

Remember not to double up by taking paracetamol alongside cold and flu remedies that also contain it, as this can easily lead to an accidental overdose

The NHS recommends gargling with salt water to relieve a sore throat, while a homemade hot lemon and honey drink can soothe a nasty cough , adds Dr Jamie Hynes, vice president of the Royal College of GPs

See a GP if a cough has lasted for more than 21 days, says Hynes, or if you've lost weight unintentionally or, in urgent cases, if experiencing chest pain or breathing difficulties

And, note some cold medicines are not suitable for pregnant women so do check with a midwife, pharmacist or GP before taking

articles.title: Sunbed firms must not downplay cancer risk, says watchdog
articles.summary: The advertising watchdog says they also must not make misleading claims that sunbeds can treat skin conditions or improve mental health.
articles.body:
A watchdog has launched a crackdown on misleading sunbed adverts, warning tanning firms they must not claim their beds are safe or can treat medical conditions.

The Committee for Advertising Practice (CAP) said it was issuing a UK-wide enforcement notice to "send a clear message to the industry that advertisers must not downplay the risks associated with sunbed use".

Earlier this year, the BBC identified hundreds of social media videos claiming the beds could boost energy and treat skin conditions or mental health problems.

The Sunbed Association, which represents around half of the UK's tanning salons, said it fully supported action against misleading adverts, but said businesses must still be allowed to demonstrate they operate responsibly.

The CAP, which draws up the UK's advertising rules, said some of the claims being made by companies were potentially harmful and could discourage customers from seeking appropriate medical treatment or advice.

"Sunbeds carry serious health risks, including an increased risk of skin cancer," said the CAP's compliance executive James Burnett.

"Ads shouldn't downplay those risks or present sunbed use as a way to improve health."

Cancer charities and doctors are clear about the risks of using sunbeds - and say the machines are linked to higher rates of melanoma and other skin cancers.

Using a bed before the age of 35 increases the risk of melanoma by 59% later in life, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).

Young people are by far the biggest sunbed users in the UK - about one in seven 18-to-24-year-olds say they used one in the past year, double the average for all age groups, according to a 2025 YouGov survey.

Rosie Vare, health information manager at Teenage Cancer Trust, said skin cancer was one of the most common forms of the disease in young adults and she welcomed stricter enforcement of the advertising rules.

"We want young people to be properly informed about the risk of sunbed use and we recommend using trusted, regulated sources to find out information such as the NHS or cancer charities ," she added.

The CAP said it had identified a series of misleading health claims in sunbed advertising, including suggestions that tanning beds can ease eczema symptoms, improve brain function, reduce inflammation and boost circulation.

Earlier this year, the Advertising Standards Authority (ASA), which enforces the CAP code, banned five adverts that claimed sunbeds could help manage conditions including osteoporosis and depression.

The new enforcement notice warns businesses not to make medical claims, promote sunbeds as a source of vitamin D or suggest sunbeds are safe.

Sunbed use is legal and regulated in all parts of the UK, with limits on the strength of the UV light the beds can emit and a ban on under-18s using the devices.

According to the Sunbed Association, its members train staff to screen out high-risk customers with very fair skin and, under its guidelines, no individual should be allowed to buy more than 60 sessions a year.

The organisation's chairman, Gary Lipman, said he would never encourage members to use health claims to promote their products.

He said he has worked with the CAP to ensure the code would not stop members explaining how they comply with regulations.

"We fully support action against misleading advertising. But there is a world of difference between claiming something is risk free and explaining that a business operates responsibly," he said.

The CAP said that advertisers have been given until 7 December 2026 to make sure any marketing claims are compliant.

It said it would be using an AI-based monitoring system to identify ads that continue to break the rules and would "take further action where needed".
